records.name: Campeche
records.current_summary: Campeche is among the Mexican states that have embraced the reform direction: its congress passed a 2024 Civil Code reform creating an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, following the national supreme court's rulings pressing states to provide one. Identity documents can therefore be aligned locally without litigation — the single most visitor-relevant legal fact in a country where mismatched documents drive questioning and denials.  Same-sex conduct is not criminalised, and no hostile state ordinances or enforcement incidents against trans people appear in the audited sources. National context remains violent for trans people, and other states' transfemicide laws (Mexico City's 2024 statute being the benchmark) frame reform elsewhere; Campeche's own record in the surviving sources is defined by its recognition procedure rather than by documented incidents.

sources.claim: HRW (31 Mar 2025) Trans Rights in Mexico, state-by-state table: 22 of Mexico's 32 states now have an administrative legal-gender-recognition procedure. Campeche's congress passed a 2024 Civil Code reform creating an administrative legal gender recognition procedure.

The Guardian (24 Jul 2024): Mexico City's congress passed the 'Paola Buenrostro law' making transfemicide a crime punishable by up to 70 years - the second of Mexico's 32 states to criminalise it, galvanised by the 2016 murder of trans sex worker Paola Buenrostro; the law obliges the attorney-general's office to publish statistics on crimes against the LGBTQ+ community.

flags: Campeche's legislature recognises the transfemicide offence

records.name: Chiapas
records.current_summary: Same-sex conduct is legal and no law targets trans presence, but Chiapas is one of ten of Mexico's 32 states whose legislatures had still created no legal gender recognition procedure as of March 2025, despite supreme-court doctrine establishing the right. The practical consequence is permanently mismatched identity documents for trans people — the single most visitor-relevant legal fact in Mexico, since document mismatch triggers questioning at checkpoints, banks and clinics — with no local administrative cure; courts can order recognition case by case.  Rights reporting on a neighbouring non-reforming state (an unsolved killing of a trans activist, health staff outting patients, no hate-motivation provisions) illustrates the institutional climate such refusal sustains, though no Chiapas-specific violence series is documented in the surviving sources. Mexico City's 2024 transfemicide law marks the reform benchmark this state has not followed.

sources.claim: HRW (31 Mar 2025) Trans Rights in Mexico, state-by-state table: 22 of Mexico's 32 states now have an administrative legal-gender-recognition procedure. Chiapas has NOT reformed its legislation to create a legal gender recognition procedure as of March 2025, leaving trans residents with mismatched documents and case-by-case judicial recourse only.

HRW (6 Mar 2024) report: in Tabasco, murders and violence against trans people have shaken the community; the state has no legal gender recognition procedure, so trans people face document-mismatch discrimination in employment, health, education and financial transactions - hospital staff called out interviewees' legal names in waiting rooms. HRW urges a simple self-identification procedure. Retained for Chiapas as the neighbouring non-reforming state's documented climate (unsolved killing of a trans activist, no hate-motivation provisions).

The Guardian (24 Jul 2024): Mexico City's congress passed the 'Paola Buenrostro law' making transfemicide a crime punishable by up to 70 years - the second of Mexico's 32 states to criminalise it, galvanised by the 2016 murder of trans sex worker Paola Buenrostro; the law obliges the attorney-general's office to publish statistics on crimes against the LGBTQ+ community.

records.name: Chihuahua
records.current_summary: Chihuahua has functioning gender-recognition machinery without a state statute: after the state civil code still required a judicial process, a 2019 supreme-court ruling struck that requirement down, and the civil registry now performs administrative recognitions. The state legislature itself had enacted no recognition law as of March 2025. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised, and no hostile state ordinance is documented in the surviving sources.  The surviving audited sources for this record document no state-specific incident series; the national backdrop for trans people remains violent and impunity-prone, with the capital's 2024 transfemicide law the reform benchmark other states are measured against.

sources.claim: HRW (31 Mar 2025) Trans Rights in Mexico, state-by-state table: 22 of Mexico's 32 states now have an administrative legal-gender-recognition procedure. Chihuahua has enacted no legislative recognition reform as of March 2025, but its Civil Registry maintains an administrative practice following the 2019 Supreme Court ruling that struck down the judicial-process requirement.

The Guardian (24 Jul 2024): Mexico City's congress passed the 'Paola Buenrostro law' making transfemicide a crime punishable by up to 70 years - the second of Mexico's 32 states to criminalise it, galvanised by the 2016 murder of trans sex worker Paola Buenrostro; the law obliges the attorney-general's office to publish statistics on crimes against the LGBTQ+ community.

records.name: Colima
records.current_summary: Colima is governed by Mexico's federal framework: same-sex conduct is not criminalised, legal gender recognition remains an unresolved state-by-state mosaic that courts have pressed legislatures to complete, and the country overall is one of Latin America's deadliest settings for trans people with high impunity, as the capital's 2024 transfemicide law reflects.  The audited record documents no Colima-specific law, procedure, ordinance or incident series.

sources.claim: National framework (HRW, 31 Mar 2025): legal gender recognition in Mexico is set state-by-state — as of March 2025, 22 of the 32 states had legislated an administrative recognition procedure, two more run one in practice without enactment, six legislatures have enacted none, and only seven states extend recognition to children. Mexico's Supreme Court set binding guidelines for the states and extended the right to minors in 2022; the Inter-American Court likewise requires a simple, accessible procedure. HRW documents the consequences where no procedure exists (identity-document mismatch driving discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, incidents recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco). For this record: the national mosaic, not any locally enacted certainty, is the operative framework.

HRW/Community Center for Inclusion report (6 Mar 2024) on a Mexican state lacking a legal gender-recognition procedure, documented in Tabasco: without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request or appearance scrutiny carries violence, harassment and humiliation risk, excluding trans people from employment, health services, education and financial transactions; context includes the Aug 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gomez in Villahermosa and more than 95% of homicides nationally going unpunished in 2022. For this record it is the operative evidence of what 'state law silent' means for trans people on the ground.

The Guardian (24 Jul 2024): Mexico City passed the 'Paola Buenrostro law' in July 2024, making transfemicide a crime punishable by up to 70 years — the second of Mexico's 32 states to criminalise it, after Nayarit (up to 60 years). In 2022 more than 95% of homicides in Mexico went unpunished, with transfemicide impunity thought higher still. For this record: benchmarks the national lethality level and the emerging transfemicide-crime trend under which the region sits.

records.name: Durango
records.current_summary: No Durango-specific laws, incidents or enforcement patterns are supported by the vetted sources for this map. The national picture governs: by March 2025 an international human-rights organization counted 22 of Mexico's 32 states as having legislated legal gender-recognition procedures, with six state legislatures enacting none; a March 2024 report from the same organization documents that where no procedure exists, trans people face police stops, denied documents and institutional mistreatment.  Transfeminicide has become a criminal category in some states — the capital imposes up to 70 years — against more than 95% homicide impunity nationally, and reporting finds convictions lag the statutes. For a visitor, Durango's own documented record is thin: expect the country-wide picture, neither verified local protections nor verified local hostility.
